analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to pay market prices for minerals, grazing, timber, and energy taken from federal land.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 1999 with 20 cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the government to stop selling the public's natural assets for less than they are worth. It would impose a 5% royalty on gold, copper, and other hardrock mining on federal land, end the sale of mining claims, charge market-rate grazing fees to ranchers on federal land, prohibit timber sales from national forests that cost taxpayers more than they bring in, and raise oil and gas lease rentals from as little as $1 per acre to fair market value. The money would help reduce the federal debt, and mining royalties would fund cleanup of abandoned mines.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently absorb the difference between below-market prices and what these resources would fetch from a private buyer, plus communities near abandoned mines that would get a funded cleanup program. Federal royalty enforcement would also benefit Native American mineral owners who lose money to underreported royalties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any department from selling timber, minerals, forage, water, or hydroelectric energy generated at federal facilities for less than fair market value.

Imposes a 5% royalty on hardrock minerals mined under the 1872 general mining laws and deposits it into an Abandoned Minerals Mine Reclamation Fund to clean up abandoned mine sites, including polluted drainage.
Ends new patents on mining claims, allowing patents only for applications filed before September 30, 1994 that met all legal requirements.
Requires annual fair-market-value grazing fees on National Forest and Bureau of Land Management lands in 16 western states, replacing fees that historically ran far below private rangeland rates.
Phases out below-cost timber sales from national forests by October 1, 2004, so the Treasury would receive more from each sale than the government spends preparing and administering it.

Raises oil and gas rentals on federal leases from fixed rates as low as $1 per acre to fair market value, adds fees for transferring federal leases, and lets the Interior Department assess a 20% penalty on underreported royalties on federal and Indian leases.
Requires farmers who receive subsidized federal irrigation water to pay the full cost of that water, and reduces their farm subsidy and disaster payment caps by the value of the water subsidy.
Directs the President's budget to list projected revenues from selling federal assets alongside what those assets would sell for in a private arms-length transaction, making the gap public each year.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies, public-lands ranchers, timber buyers, oil and gas lessees, utilities holding rights-of-way across public land, and large farmers receiving subsidized federal irrigation water, all of whom would see their costs rise toward market rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Miners, ranchers, timber and energy companies

drawbacks.text: Higher prices for grazing, timber, minerals, and water would feed into consumer costs for food, lumber, paper, and minerals, though the point of the bill is that those prices are now being partly paid by taxpayers instead.

The bill repeals the Emergency Livestock Feed Assistance program and cuts disaster and price-support payments for farms that receive subsidized irrigation water, reducing the farm safety net for some producers rather than only ending subsidies to the largest operators.
Existing contracts, leases, and arrangements are grandfathered, and new ones signed within five years of enactment would keep below-market pricing for up to five years, delaying most of the savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: companies would pay closer to what federal resources are actually worth, and taxpayers would stop subsidizing them. The cost would show up as somewhat higher prices for wood, food, and minerals and a thinner livestock disaster program. The bill's own grandfathering of existing deals, and its five-year delay for new ones, weakens how much revenue it would actually raise. On balance the public would come out ahead, which is what makes its quiet death worth attention.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three committees and then split among seven subcommittees, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Representative George Miller of California introduced the bill on June 15, 1999, joined by 19 Democratic colleagues as original cosponsors.

It was referred to the Resources, Agriculture, and Budget Committees, then divided among seven subcommittees covering energy and minerals, parks, water and power, forests, and farm commodities by the end of June 1999.
No further action of any kind was taken on the bill through the end of the 106th Congress on January 3, 2001, meaning no committee ever reported it out and the House never voted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies, public-lands ranchers, timber buyers, and oil and gas lessees kept receiving federal minerals, forage, timber, and leases at below-market rates, while taxpayers continued covering the difference and the costs of abandoned mine damage.

for.name: Rep. George Miller (D-CA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Public Resources Debt Reduction Act of 1999 and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.

for.name: 20 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

against.name: Rep. Don Young (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which sat in the Resources Committee and its subcommittees for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Larry Combest (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled action on the bill's farm, grazing, and irrigation provisions, which were referred to three Agriculture subcommittees.

against.name: Rep. John Kasich (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled action on the bill's debt-reduction and budget-disclosure provisions.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken; all 21 sponsors were House Democrats, and the bill died without action in committees chaired by Republicans.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, copper, silver and other locatable minerals)
industries.note: Mining under the 1872 general mining law lets companies extract hardrock minerals from federal land with no royalty and, historically, patent the land itself for a nominal price. The bill would charge a 5% royalty, end new patents, and add claim fees, with the revenue funding cleanup of abandoned mine sites the public otherwise pays for.

Federal grazing fees have historically been set far below what comparable private rangeland charges. The bill would require fair-market-value fees on Forest Service and BLM lands, ending a subsidy paid by taxpayers.

The bill would ban sales of national forest timber that return less to the Treasury than they cost to prepare and administer, phasing them out by 2004. Buyers of cheap federal timber would face fewer sales and higher prices.

industries.industry: Oil and gas lessees on federal land
industries.note: Fixed rentals as low as $1 per acre would be replaced with market-rate rentals, lease transfers would carry fees, and underreporting royalties on federal and Indian leases would draw a 20% assessment.

industries.industry: Farms receiving subsidized federal irrigation water
industries.note: These operations would have to pay full cost for reclamation-project water and would have their crop subsidy and disaster payment caps cut by the value of the water subsidy, ending a double benefit.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and other users of federal hydropower and rights-of-way
industries.note: Federal hydropower could no longer be sold below market value, and holders of rights-of-way for power lines, pipelines, and water conveyances across public land would pay annual fair-market-value fees.
